claim: John Snow ended the 1854 cholera outbreak in London by removing a pump handle.

heard.who: London Museum, 'John Snow: Cholera & the Broad Street pump'
heard.quote: Snow convinced the local authorities to remove the pump handle, stopping people from using it. The cholera outbreak subsided.

heard.who: JSTOR Daily, article by Matthew Wills
heard.quote: The water pump's handle was removed to render it inoperable. Cases of cholera plummeted afterwards.

answer: Partly. In 1854 Snow plotted Soho's cholera deaths on a map and found them clustered around the Broad Street pump, and the authorities removed its handle after he took his findings to them. The outbreak had already peaked a week earlier, so removing the handle was not what first turned it around.

facts.text: In the 1854 Soho cholera outbreak, John Snow plotted the deaths on a map, and they clustered around the water pump on Broad Street (now Broadwick Street).

sources.title: John Snow: Cholera & the Broad Street pump
sources.quote: The map showed clearly that the deaths were clustered around a water pump on Broad Street, now Broadwick Street.

sources.title: John Snow Hunts the Blue Death
sources.quote: the eye is immediately drawn toward the thick black lines clustering around the epicenter, the location of the Broad Street water pump

sources.title: John Snow and the Birth of Epidemiology
sources.quote: What united all the cases? They got their water at this Broad Street pump in the Soho neighborhood.

facts.text: After Snow took his findings to the local authorities, the handle of the Broad Street pump was removed.

sources.title: John Snow: Cholera & the Broad Street pump
sources.quote: Snow convinced the local authorities to remove the pump handle, stopping people from using it. The cholera outbreak subsided.

sources.title: John Snow Hunts the Blue Death
sources.quote: Ultimately, it was an impressive enough case to convince the parish government to remove the pump's handle.

sources.title: John Snow and the Birth of Epidemiology
sources.quote: The water pump's handle was removed to render it inoperable. Cases of cholera plummeted afterwards.

facts.text: The outbreak had already passed its peak before the handle was removed: deaths peaked on 1 September 1854 and the handle came off on 8 September.

sources.title: Cholera and a tale of two cities
sources.quote: Sidney Chave's tabulation of the daily cases illustrates how the epidemic had already peaked on 1 September, whereas Snow removed the handle off the pump on 8 September.

sources.publisher: UCLA Department of Epidemiology, John Snow site (quoting the Rev. Henry Whitehead)
sources.title: Stream 2: Handle Removal, Index Case and Rev. Whitehead
sources.quote: the outbreak had already reached its climax, and had been steadily on the decline for several days before the pump-handle was removed.

sources.title: Broad Street Cholera Pump
sources.quote: In reality, the outbreak was already in decline, and the specific contamination that had triggered the outbreak had probably come and gone.

contested.text: Whether removing the handle ended the outbreak. The Rev. Henry Whitehead said that the outbreak had already run its course, and that removing the handle probably prevented a new outbreak instead.

sources.publisher: UCLA Department of Epidemiology, John Snow site (quoting the Rev. Henry Whitehead)
sources.title: Stream 2: Handle Removal, Index Case and Rev. Whitehead
sources.quote: I must not omit to mention that if the removal of the pump-handle had nothing to do with checking the outbreak which had already run its course, it had probably everything to do with preventing a new outbreak

could_not_verify: Snow's own 1855 report, read directly; the accounts cited quote or describe it.
A count of how many lives the handle removal saved, if any.
not_claimed: That Snow's map proved how cholera spreads; this card covers only the 1854 pump.
That the handle's removal made no difference at all.
